steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction (with a short related-work subsection) for our robotics/vision paper on visual planning that combines concept-based disentangled representation learning, symbolic reasoning and causal transition modeling. Explain the motivation, the gaps in prior approaches, our framework and dataset, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Planning and visual planning: what they are and why they matter
- Prior visual planning approaches and their limits; our three components
- Why concept-based representations and atomic causal transitions
- Our framework: three modules, plus a new dataset
- Contributions
- Related work: visual planning; concept-based disentangled representations; causal reasoning

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Planning and visual planning
  - planning = fundamental ability of human intelligence; proposing sequence of actions toward goals
  - needs thinking ahead, knowledge of causality, imagination (cite); foresee actions + consequences on states for all intermediate steps
  - visual planning: search for visual transitions between initial visual state and final visual goal state
  - guides agents in daily tasks, first-person view -> important in egocentric vision (cite) and embodied AI
  - robotics: avoids manually designing goal conditions, action preconditions, effects
- Prior approaches and our components
  - three tracks: neural-network-based (cite), RL-based (cite), classic search-based (cite)
  - NN-based: end-to-end, weak interpretability (cite)
  - RL-based: goal-conditioned decisions, but sparse reward, low data efficiency (cite), low environment/task generalization (cite)
  - ours: search-based, inspired by human cognition; three components = representation learning, symbolic reasoning, causal transition modeling
  - representation learning -> objects' dynamic, goal-oriented attributes; symbolic reasoning -> planning at abstract level via learned symbols; causal transition -> visual preconditions + action effects on attributes
- Representations and causal transitions
  - perception level: concept-based disentangled representation; abstracting concepts vital for visual causal transition modeling (cite)
  - encodes images above pixels, distinct attribute concepts, isolates "essential" factors of variation -> serves causal learning (cite)
  - robustness + interpretability (cite); compositional zero-shot generalization (cite)
  - reasoning level: atomic causal mechanisms needed for task planning; identify relevant variable concepts, predict outcomes of actions
  - higher-level planning built from atomic transitions -> more generalizable, interpretable (cite)
  - vict + abstracted symbolic transition model: discrete high-level planning, avoids "error accumulation" (cite)
  - visual transition reconstructs intermediate and final goal images
- Framework and dataset
  - module 1: scl (Sec. III-A), switching latent concept representations of image pairs with different attribute concepts
  - module 2: state symbols from clustering low-level concept token representations (Sec. III-B); best symbolic path via MDP
  - module 3: visual transition model (Sec. III-C): action-induced transition of changeable attributes from precondition image -> effect image
  - large-scale visual planning dataset: concept learning dataset + causal planning dataset
  - comparisons + ablations: superior performance in planning and generalization tests
- Contributions
  - (i) concept-based visual planning framework, discrete symbolic + continuous visual transition; superior performance in planning and generalization
  - (ii) interpretability: causal chain (action sequences + intermediate state images) shows transition to the goal
  - (iii) large-scale visual planning dataset for the community
## I-A Related Work
- Visual planning
  - possible with learned representation + atomic causal effects
  - long-horizon deformable object manipulation (cite) - relies on differentiable physics simulators
  - tree-search planning on learned world representation for visual robot task planning (cite) - no disentangled representations
  - goal-directed planning from real-world instructional videos (cite) - transformer end-to-end, hard to generalize
  - encoding / action-conditional transformation / decoding for Atari video prediction (cite) - no symbols
  - most similar: symbolic operators for task and motion planning (cite) - no intermediate images
- Concept-based disentangled representation learning
  - popular for human-interpretable representations (cite)
  - discrete, semantically-grounded -> human understanding, abstract visual reasoning, few/zero-shot, downstream performance (cite)
  - unsupervised (cite); weak supervision + implicit prototypes (cite); linguistic supervision (cite)

  - ours: variant of the Transformer approach with more reconstruction constraints; complex household objects (Sec. II); better for planning

  - essential human capability; big challenge for AI - situated actions, dependencies, causal effects on object states (cite)
  - SOTA models good on descriptive, poor on explanatory/predictive/counterfactual -> need disentangled grounded perception + hierarchical causal relations and dynamics (cite)
  - sequential Causal And-Or Graph (C-AOG) (cite) - ambiguity from poorly disentangled representation
  - ours: latent space isolating important factors from confounders (cite); actions grounded to effects on attributes; bi-level framework resists noise and ambiguity

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Planning is one of the fundamental abilities of human intelligence. It is the process of coming up with a sequence of actions to reach desired goals, and it needs the ability to think ahead, to use knowledge of causality, and imagination, so that one can reason about and foresee the right actions and their consequences on the states for all the intermediate transition steps until the goal state is reached. Visual planning simulates this process of sequential causal imagination as a search for visual transitions between an initial visual state and a final visual goal state. Because it can guide agents to do daily tasks in the first-person view, visual planning has become more and more important in egocentric vision and embodied AI. In robotics, visual planning could also avoid having to manually design the specific goal conditions, action preconditions, and effects needed for robots.

Previous works on visual planning can be roughly divided into three tracks: neural-network-based models, reinforcement-learning-based models and classic search-based models. Neural-network-based models can be trained end-to-end, but they tend to fall short on interpretability. Reinforcement-learning-based models can make goal-conditioned decisions, but they can suffer from sparse reward, low data efficiency, and low generalization to new environments and tasks. Because of these limitations, and inspired by human cognition, our method is in the third, search-based category, and we propose three key components for visual planning: representation learning, symbolic reasoning, and causal transition modeling. Representation learning extracts the dynamic and goal-oriented attributes of objects. Symbolic reasoning does action planning at the abstract higher level using learned symbols. Causal transition models the visual preconditions and the effects of actions on attribute changes.

At the perception level, we propose to learn a concept-based disentangled representation. We believe this human-like ability to abstract concepts from observations is vital for modeling visual causal transitions. This is because such representation learning can encode images at a higher semantic level than pixels, identify distinct attribute concepts and isolate the “essential” factors of variation, which serves causal learning. It also improves robustness and interpretability, and it helps compositional generalization to unseen scenarios in zero-shot inference, so it supports many real-world downstream tasks. At the reasoning and planning level, we argue that understanding the atomic causal mechanisms is necessary for task planning. Using the learned disentangled concept representations, we get insight into the core of atomic causal transitions, which means identifying the key relevant variable concepts and predicting the outcomes of the actions done on them. Understanding and reasoning about abstract higher-level task planning that is made of lower-level atomic causal transitions could also be more generalizable and interpretable. So we propose vict and its abstracted symbolic transition model, which corresponds to the discrete higher-level task planning and avoids the problem of “error accumulation”. With the symbolic transition as guidance, the visual transition reconstructs the intermediate and final goal images.

  - module 1: scl (Sec. III-A), switching latent concept representations of image pairs with different attribute concepts
  - module 2: state symbols from clustering low-level concept token representations (Sec. III-B); best symbolic path via MDP
  - module 3: visual transition model (Sec. III-C): action-induced transition of changeable attributes from precondition image -> effect image
  - large-scale visual planning dataset: concept learning dataset + causal planning dataset
  - comparisons + ablations: superior performance in planning and generalization tests

- Contributions
  - (i) concept-based visual planning framework, discrete symbolic + continuous visual transition; superior performance in planning and generalization
  - (ii) interpretability: causal chain (action sequences + intermediate state images) shows transition to the goal
  - (iii) large-scale visual planning dataset for the community

  - goal-directed planning from real-world instructional videos (cite) - transformer end-to-end, hard to generalize
  - encoding / action-conditional transformation / decoding for Atari video prediction (cite) - no symbols
  - most similar: symbolic operators for task and motion planning (cite) - no intermediate images

  - popular for human-interpretable representations (cite)
  - discrete, semantically-grounded -> human understanding, abstract visual reasoning, few/zero-shot, downstream performance (cite)
  - unsupervised (cite); weak supervision + implicit prototypes (cite); linguistic supervision (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Planning is one of the fundamental abilities of human intelligence. It is the process of coming up with a sequence of actions to reach desired goals, and it needs the ability to think ahead, to use knowledge of causality, and imagination, so that one can reason about and foresee the right actions and their consequences on the states for all the intermediate transition steps until the goal state is reached. Visual planning simulates this process of sequential causal imagination as a search for visual transitions between an initial visual state and a final visual goal state. Because it can guide agents to do daily tasks in the first-person view, visual planning has become more and more important in egocentric vision and embodied AI. In robotics, visual planning could also avoid having to manually design the specific goal conditions, action preconditions, and effects needed for robots.

Previous works on visual planning can be roughly divided into three tracks: neural-network-based models, reinforcement-learning-based models and classic search-based models. Neural-network-based models can be trained end-to-end, but they tend to fall short on interpretability. Reinforcement-learning-based models can make goal-conditioned decisions, but they can suffer from sparse reward, low data efficiency, and low generalization to new environments and tasks. Because of these limitations, and inspired by human cognition, our method is in the third, search-based category, and we propose three key components for visual planning: representation learning, symbolic reasoning, and causal transition modeling. Representation learning extracts the dynamic and goal-oriented attributes of objects. Symbolic reasoning does action planning at the abstract higher level using learned symbols. Causal transition models the visual preconditions and the effects of actions on attribute changes.

At the perception level, we propose to learn a concept-based disentangled representation. We believe this human-like ability to abstract concepts from observations is vital for modeling visual causal transitions. This is because such representation learning can encode images at a higher semantic level than pixels, identify distinct attribute concepts and isolate the “essential” factors of variation, which serves causal learning. It also improves robustness and interpretability, and it helps compositional generalization to unseen scenarios in zero-shot inference, so it supports many real-world downstream tasks. At the reasoning and planning level, we argue that understanding the atomic causal mechanisms is necessary for task planning. Using the learned disentangled concept representations, we get insight into the core of atomic causal transitions, which means identifying the key relevant variable concepts and predicting the outcomes of the actions done on them. Understanding and reasoning about abstract higher-level task planning that is made of lower-level atomic causal transitions could also be more generalizable and interpretable. So we propose vict and its abstracted symbolic transition model, which corresponds to the discrete higher-level task planning and avoids the problem of “error accumulation”. With the symbolic transition as guidance, the visual transition reconstructs the intermediate and final goal images.

Technically, our visual planning framework has three critical modules. First, a new scl (Sec. III-A) is learned by switching the latent concept representations of a pair of images that have different attribute concepts. Second, we abstract a set of state symbols by clustering low-level concept token representations (Sec. III-B), and the most efficient symbolic transition path can be found with a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Third, we propose a visual transition model (Sec. III-C) that learns the action-induced transition of the changeable attributes given the concept representations of the precondition image, and so generates the resulting effect image. To check that our framework is effective, we collect a large-scale visual planning dataset, which has a concept learning dataset and a causal planning dataset. Extensive comparison experiments and ablation studies on this dataset show that our model achieves superior performance on the visual planning task and on different kinds of generalization tests.

Our main contributions are: (i) We propose a new concept-based visual planning framework that models both discrete symbolic transition and continuous visual transition, for efficient path search and for generating intermediate images. Comprehensive experiments show that our method gets superior performance in visual task planning and generalization tests. (ii) Besides generalizability, our method is more interpretable because it generates a causal chain (the action sequences and the intermediate state images) that explicitly shows the transition process to the goal. (iii) We collect a large-scale visual planning dataset that can help future research in the community.

## I-A Related Work

Visual planning is possible with the learned representation and atomic causal effects. One work proposed a method for long-horizon deformable object manipulation tasks from sensory observations, but it relies heavily on differentiable physics simulators. Another work did tree-search-based planning on the learned world representation after applying high-level actions for visual robot task planning, but it ignored learning disentangled representations. Another learned to plan a goal-directed decision-making procedure from real-world videos, using structured and plannable latent state and action spaces learned from human instructional videos, but its transformer-based end-to-end model is hard to generalize to unseen planning tasks. Another proposed a model based on deep neural networks with encoding, action-conditional transformation, and decoding for video prediction in Atari Games, but it does not abstract symbols for efficient reasoning. The work most similar to ours learned symbolic operators for task and motion planning, but it cannot generate intermediate images.

Concept-based disentangled representation learning has become a popular way to extract human-interpretable representations. It is argued that discrete and semantically-grounded representations help human understanding and abstract visual reasoning, enable few-shot or zero-shot learning, and lead to better downstream task performance. Previous studies tried to learn disentangled concept representations either in a completely unsupervised way, or with weak supervision and implicit prototype representations, or with supervision from the linguistic space. Many different learning techniques have been used, such as Transformer, (sequential) variational autoencoder, and information maximizing generative adversarial nets, etc. Existing techniques have worked on objects with mostly limited variation, like digits, simple geometric objects, and faces. In this work, we propose a variant of the Transformer-based approach with more reconstruction constraints, which works very well on more complex household objects with diverse variations (Sec. II) and helps the downstream planning task more than prior works.

Causal reasoning for task understanding is one of the essential capabilities of human intelligence, and it is a big challenge for AI because it is hard to generate a detailed understanding of situated actions, their dependencies, and their causal effects on object states. Various state-of-the-art models that were evaluated only do well on the perception-based descriptive task, and do poorly on the causal tasks (i.e., explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual tasks). This suggests that a principled approach for causal reasoning should include not only disentangled and semantically grounded visual perception, but also the underlying hierarchical causal relations and dynamics. Another work built a sequential Causal And-Or Graph (C-AOG) to represent actions and their effects on objects over time, but it suffers from ambiguity in real-life images because its representation is not well disentangled. Our work benefits from our disentangled concept representation, because it finds a latent space where important factors can be isolated from other confounding factors, and we ground actions to their causal effects on relevant object attributes. Our bi-level causal planning framework, with discrete symbolic transition and continuous visual transition, also helps to resist noise and ambiguity in real-world data.

steps.text:
As one of the fundamental abilities of human intelligence, planning is the process of proposing a sequence of actions to achieve desired goals, which requires the capacity to think ahead, to employ knowledge of causality, and the capacity of imagination [1], so as to reason about and foresee the proper actions and their consequences on the states for all intermediate transition steps before finally reaching the goal state. Visual planning simulates this thinking process of sequential causal imagination in the form of searching for visual transitions between an initial visual state and a final visual goal state. With its advantages in guiding agents to perform daily tasks in the first-person view, visual planning has become increasingly important in egocentric vision [2] and embodied AI. In robotics, visual planning could also avoid manually designing the specific goal conditions, action preconditions, and effects required for robots.

Previous works for visual planning can be roughly categorized into three tracks, i.e., neural-network-based models [3,4], reinforcement-learning-based models [5,6] and classic search-based models [7,8]. Neural-network-based models can be trained in an end-to-end manner, but tend to fall short in terms of interpretability [9]. Reinforcement-learning-based models can perform goal-conditioned decisions, but could suffer from sparse reward, low data efficiency [10], and low environment and task generalization ability [11]. Considering these limitations and inspired by human cognition, our method falls into the third "search-based" category and further proposes three key components for visual planning, namely representation learning, symbolic reasoning, and causal transition modeling. Representation learning focuses on extracting objects' dynamic and goal-oriented attributes. Symbolic reasoning performs action planning at the abstract higher level via learned symbols. Causal transition models the visual preconditions and action effects on attribute changes.

At the perception level, we propose to learn a concept-based disentangled representation, and we believe such a human-like perception ability to abstract concepts from observations is vital for visual causal transition modeling [12]. The reason is that such representation learning can encode images at a higher semantic level beyond pixels, identifying distinct attribute concepts and isolating "essential" factors of variation, thus serving causal learning [13]. This also enhances both robustness and interpretability [14,13,15], and facilitates compositional generalization to unseen scenarios in zero-shot inference [16,13,17,18], thereby supporting a wide range of real-world downstream tasks. At the reasoning and planning level, we argue that understanding the atomic causal mechanisms is inevitable for task planning. Leveraging the learned disentangled representations of concepts, we gain insight into the core of atomic causal transitions, which involves identifying key relevant variable concepts and predicting the outcomes of actions executed upon them. The understanding and reasoning of abstract higher-level task planning composed of lower-level atomic causal transitions also has the potential to be more generalizable and interpretable [19,20]. Thus, we propose vict and its abstracted symbolic transition model, which corresponds to the discrete higher-level task planning and avoids the problem of "error accumulation" [21]. Guided by the symbolic transition, the visual transition reconstructs intermediate and final goal images.

Technically, there are three critical modules in our visual planning framework. First, a novel scl (Sec. III-A) is learned by switching the latent concept representations of a pair of images with different attribute concepts. Second, a set of state symbols is abstracted by clustering low-level concept token representations (Sec. III-B), and the most efficient symbolic transition path can be found via a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Third, a visual transition model (Sec. III-C) is proposed to learn the action-induced transition of the changeable attributes given the concept representations of the precondition image, and thus generate the resulting effect image. To verify the effectiveness of our framework, we collect a large-scale visual planning dataset, which contains a concept learning dataset and a causal planning dataset. Extensive comparison experiments and ablation studies on this dataset demonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in the visual planning task and in various forms of generalization tests.

To summarize, our main contributions are: (i) We propose a novel concept-based visual planning framework, which models both discrete symbolic transition and continuous visual transition for efficient path search and intermediate image generation. Comprehensive experiments show that our method achieves superior performance in visual task planning and generalization tests. (ii) Apart from generalizability, our method has better interpretability, generating a causal chain (the action sequences and the intermediate state images) that explicitly demonstrates the transition process to the goal. (iii) We collect a large-scale visual planning dataset, which can foster future research in the community.

## I-A Related Work

Visual planning is feasible with the learned representation and atomic causal effects. [22] proposed a method for long-horizon deformable object manipulation tasks from sensory observations, which relies heavily on differentiable physics simulators. [7] performed a tree-search-based planning algorithm on the learned world representation after applying high-level actions for visual robot task planning, but ignored learning disentangled representations. [3] learned to plan a goal-directed decision-making procedure from real-world videos, leveraging structured and plannable latent state and action spaces learned from human instructional videos, but their transformer-based end-to-end model is hard to generalize to unseen planning tasks. [4] proposed a model based on deep neural networks consisting of encoding, action-conditional transformation, and decoding for video prediction in Atari Games, but it does not abstract symbols for efficient reasoning. [23] is the most similar to ours; it learned symbolic operators for task and motion planning, but cannot generate intermediate images.

Concept-based disentangled representation learning has emerged as a popular way of extracting human-interpretable representations [24]. Discrete and semantically-grounded representations are argued to be helpful for human understanding and abstract visual reasoning, to enable few-shot or zero-shot learning, and to lead to better downstream task performance [25,26]. Previous studies tried to learn disentangled concept representations either in a completely unsupervised manner [27,28,29,30], or via weak supervision and implicit prototype representations [31], or by employing supervision from the linguistic space [32,33]. There have been diverse learning techniques, such as Transformer [30], (sequential) variational autoencoder [28,29], and information maximizing generative adversarial nets [27], etc. Existing techniques have proved successful mostly on objects with limited variation, such as digits, simple geometric objects [31], and faces [27]. In this work, we propose a variant of [30] that imposes more reconstruction constraints, which works very well on more complex household objects with diverse variations (Sec. II) and better benefits the downstream planning task compared to prior works.

Causal reasoning for task understanding is one of the essential capabilities of human intelligence, and a big challenge for AI given the difficulty of generating a detailed understanding of situated actions, their dependencies, and their causal effects on object states [34]. Various state-of-the-art models evaluated only thrive on the perception-based descriptive task but perform poorly on the causal tasks (i.e., explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual tasks), suggesting that a principled approach to causal reasoning should incorporate not only disentangled and semantically grounded visual perception, but also the underlying hierarchical causal relations and dynamics [35]. [36] built a sequential Causal And-Or Graph (C-AOG) to represent actions and their effects on objects over time, but it suffers from ambiguity in real-life images due to its not-well-disentangled representation. Our work benefits from our disentangled concept representation by finding a latent space where important factors can be isolated from other confounding factors [16], and we ground actions to their causal effects on relevant object attributes. Our bi-level causal planning framework with discrete symbolic transition and continuous visual transition also helps to resist real-world data noise and ambiguity.
